strengths: Significant dataset contribution: PETAR-11K is the first large-scale PET/CT dataset with 11,356 lesion-level descriptions paired with 3D segmentation masks and structured annotations, addressing a genuine gap in medical imaging resources

Well-motivated architecture design with elegant solutions to domain challenges: focal prompting mechanism effectively addresses information loss from small lesions (<1% of volume), and additive mask conditioning provides clean integration of spatial information

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: multiple metric categories (NLP, semantic, LM-based), human evaluation by board-certified nuclear medicine physicians, correlation analysis identifying clinically-aligned metrics, and detailed ablation studies demonstrating component contributions

Strong and consistent empirical results: PETAR-4B outperforms all baselines across metrics with substantial improvements in clinically-relevant measures (CIDEr +0.283, GREEN +0.175) indicating superior content diversity and clinical reasoning quality

Thoughtful problem formulation demonstrating deep domain understanding: paper articulates specific PET challenges (volumetric complexity, dispersed small lesions, lengthy/variable reports) and addresses them systematically through design choices
weaknesses: Critical evaluation limitation: Single-institution evaluation severely constrains generalization claims. No cross-institutional validation despite known variations in PET reporting styles, protocols, and equipment across centers—essential for clinical deployment

Dataset quality and extraction pipeline transparency issues: mask generation via simple iterative thresholding lacks validation; no inter-rater agreement analysis; exact LLM prompts and filtering criteria relegated to supplementary material; no manual spot-checking of extracted descriptions against original reports

Potential train/test data contamination: pretraining on TotalSegmentator applied to the same CT volumes as downstream task may cause data leakage; train/test split methodology (patient-level vs. exam-level) not clearly specified

Limited technical novelty: mask-aware conditioning directly extends Reg2RG from 2D to 3D; focal prompting closely follows cited prior work [8,13]; four-stage training is standard practice. Architecture is primarily an engineering combination of existing techniques rather than methodologically novel

Incomplete robustness analysis: no evaluation of performance degradation with imperfect upstream lesion detection masks; no sensitivity analysis for focal prompt perturbation magnitude; no systematic error analysis or failure mode discussion; only 2 qualitative examples in Figure 4, with unexplained anatomical misclassification in first example

Experimental limitations undermine claims: single experimental run without confidence intervals or variance estimates; potentially suboptimal baseline adaptations (Med3DVLM performs suspiciously poorly at 0.004 BLEU); human evaluation limited (100 pairs in first round, 80 assessments in second); no inter-rater reliability (Cohen's κ) reported

Limited generalization scope: only 4 PET radiotracers covered despite many more in clinical use; no cross-tracer validation; unclear how well model generalizes to body regions beyond those in training; structured text format (region, organ, subsite, report) may artificially simplify task

Reproducibility and practical deployment concerns: dataset public availability not confirmed; proprietary model dependencies (Qwen3-30B-A3B) without specified checkpoints; no code release mentioned; critical details in supplementary material; inference time, memory footprint, and deployment feasibility not discussed; training requires 20 hours on specialized GPUs

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: PET automated reporting is clinically significant yet severely underrepresented in medical VLM research

Novel and valuable dataset contribution: PETARSeg-11K is the first public dataset combining lesion-level textual findings, 3D segmentation masks, and whole-body PET/CT volumes (11,356 lesions from 5,126 exams)
First human evaluation of automated PET reporting by board-certified physicians, establishing correlations between automated metrics (GREEN ρ=0.592) and expert judgment
Thoughtfully designed architecture addressing PET-specific challenges: focal prompting for sub-0.1% volume lesions, mask-aware dual-modality encoding, and three-stage training strategy
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple metric categories (n-gram, semantic, LLM-based) with both internal and external validation on autoPET dataset
Strong empirical improvements over 2D and 3D baselines (e.g., GREEN +0.186 vs best 3D model, ROUGE +0.070 vs best 2D model)
Rigorous ablation study demonstrating contribution of each component; focal prompt provides largest impact
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem statement and thorough supplementary material including cohort statistics and implementation details
weaknesses: Mask input dependency without robustness validation: model requires pre-segmented lesions, but no experiments test performance with automated masks or noise injection. Practical deployment requires automated segmentation but this is unvalidated

Meaningful performance gap to clinical utility: human evaluation shows PETAR-4B (3.7–3.9) versus ground truth (4.3–4.4); physicians preferred human-written findings in 47% of cases, limiting clinical acceptability

Limited architectural novelty: components largely combine existing techniques (3D ViT from M3D, focal prompt adapted from Describe Anything Model, mask conditioning similar to Reg2RG). Main contribution is task-specific application rather than methodological innovation

Quantitative hallucination problem unaddressed: model hallucinates lesion size and SUVmax values; human evaluation explicitly excluded these errors, yet they require manual correction in clinical workflow, reducing automation benefit

Modest dataset scale and limited generalization: 5,126 exams from single institution (2010–2013), single manufacturer (GE), four radiotracers only; external validation limited to 32 autoPET samples; temporal/center-specific bias possible

Insufficient human evaluation statistics: only 5 physicians with no inter-rater reliability metrics (Cohen's kappa), no confidence intervals or significance testing on preference statistics (116 sample size limits power)
Incomplete model comparisons: Pet2Rep (direct PET findings baseline) not compared; missing recent CT-based VLM comparisons; unclear whether PETAR's gains are due to architecture or dataset

Focal prompt design under-explored: random perturbation range (±20%) not justified; no ablation on magnitude; sensitivity to very small lesions (<0.01% volume) and cross-inference consistency not analyzed

Technical clarity gaps: spatial pooling operation not detailed; inference time/computational cost not reported; handling of multiple lesions per exam unclear; whether lesions have inter-lesion context

Missing error analysis and failure mode characterization: no systematic breakdown of which anatomical regions or lesion types are hardest; dataset mask generation (98% accuracy) has 2% error rate with unclear impact on model learning
